questions.topic: Separate rows from the two-index form
questions.learningObjective: trace that new int[rows][cols] allocates one distinct row per slot

options.text: "false false" and then "[0, 0, 0, 0]", because the two-index form gives every slot its own row.
"true false" and then "[7, 0, 0, 0]", because the two-index form hands out one shared row.
options.misconception: believes the two-index new form makes every slot point at the same row

options.text: "false false" and then "[7, 0, 0, 0]", because the rows have separate identities but shared cells.
options.misconception: believes separately allocated rows still share one block of cells

options.text: It throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the first line, because a partial fill narrows the grid.
options.misconception: believes writing one cell invalidates the width the allocation promised

questions.explanation: The rule is that new int[3][4] allocates three separate int[4] arrays and stores one reference to each in the outer array, so g[0] == g[1] and g[0] == g[2] are both false and the untouched row 1 still holds four zeros. Believing one row is shared is tempting because the one-index form new int[n][] does leave every slot null, and it is easy to carry that picture across, but that form has to be given rows one at a time whereas the two-index form does the inner allocation itself and gives each slot its own array.

options.text: 2, false, 0, then 0: two rows exist and each of them has width zero.
It throws NullPointerException on the second line, because no cells were allocated at all.

options.text: 0, true, 0, then 0, because a zero width means there are no rows to count either.
options.misconception: believes a zero inner dimension collapses the outer dimension as well

options.text: 2, false, 2, then 2, because each empty row still counts as one cell wide.
options.misconception: believes a row of length zero still contributes a single cell

questions.explanation: The rule is that the two-index form always creates the rows it promises, so new int[2][0] produces two non-null references to zero-length arrays: g.length is 2, g[0] == null is false, g[0].length is 0, and the loop adds nothing, so cells is 0. options.text: It prints 0 0 0 7 8 and then throws NullPointerException on the sixth read of the short row.

questions.topic: Swapping a row through a final parameter

grid = new int[1][2];  a final parameter may still be pointed at a freshly allocated grid.
options.misconception: believes final on a parameter still permits reassigning the reference

options.text: final int[] row = grid[0]; row[0] = 9;  a final local can be written through without a cast.
options.misconception: believes writing one cell through a final local replaces the whole row

options.text: grid[0][0] = 9; grid[0][1] = 9;  both cells of the caller's row can be assigned in place.
options.misconception: believes filling the old row's cells makes the old row object unreachable

true, true, then 1: the literal stored one row twice, so both slots name that same array.

options.text: false, false, then 4, because Arrays.equals compares references rather than cell values.

questions.topic: Row widths produced by splitting a line
questions.learningObjective: predict the row widths a comma split yields for lines with trailing separators

2 [7, 8], then 2 [3, ], then 2 [ ], because every separator always yields a field of its own.
options.misconception: believes a trailing comma always creates one more empty field

options.text: 3 [7, 8, ], then 2 [3, ], then 1 [ ], because split returns one field per separator plus one.
options.misconception: believes the field count is always the separator count plus one

options.text: 2 [7, 8], then 1 [3], then 1 [ ], because a line of only separators still gives one field.
options.misconception: believes a line of nothing but separators yields a single empty field

Expecting a field per separator is tempting because the separator count looks like a field count, but the default limit throws away trailing empties, which is why a ragged row built this way can arrive shorter than the file's columns suggest, and why the limit -1 is the form that keeps them.
questions.hint: Trailing empty fields are removed unless the limit says otherwise.

questions.topic: Keeping a trailing empty field
questions.learningObjective: select the split limit that preserves a field the default call discards

options.text: line.split(",", -1)  a negative limit keeps the empty fields that end the result.
line.split(",", 0)  a limit of zero is what preserves the trailing empty field.
options.misconception: believes the limit of zero is the call that keeps trailing empties

options.text: line.split(",", 1)  a limit of one still returns both fields of a line this short.
options.misconception: believes a limit of one splits on every comma in the line

options.text: line.split(",")  the one-argument form keeps a trailing empty field of its own.
options.misconception: believes the one-argument split preserves a trailing empty field

"2 26", because the width should have been seeded from the first row instead of from zero.
options.misconception: believes the widest row is found by starting the measure at row 0's width

options.text: It throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 2 out of bounds for length 2, because 3 is not a bound every row shares.

options.text: "3 32", because the cells the guard skips are still added to the total as zero-valued cells.

questions.topic: Sorting a row without disturbing the caller
questions.learningObjective: choose how to sort a caller's row in place while leaving the caller's data alone
questions.stem: A utility receives an int[] row out of a caller's grid and must return it in ascending order without changing the caller's grid. Arrays.sort is available. Which approach meets both requirements?

options.text: Sort a copy, so call Arrays.sort on Arrays.copyOf(row, row.length) and the caller's row is untouched.
Sort the row directly, because a method that receives a reference owns the array it was given.
options.misconception: believes receiving a reference transfers ownership of the array

options.text: Sort a new zero-filled array of the row's length, because zeros are the only safe values to sort.
options.misconception: believes a fresh array of the right length carries the values to be sorted

questions.topic: Following the greedy ascent across a grid
questions.learningObjective: trace a walk that steps only to a strictly larger neighbour

options.text: 0,0 then 0,1, 1,1, 2,1, 2,2 and finally "steps 4 last 9": the below cell beat the right one at 1,1.
0,0 then 0,1, 1,1, 1,2, 1,3 and finally "steps 4 last 8": the walk keeps going right along a row.
options.misconception: believes the walk follows a row rightward while the next column rises

options.text: 0,0 then 1,0, 1,1, 1,2, 2,2, 3,2, 3,3 and finally "steps 6 last 10": the climb finds the best cell.
options.misconception: believes a greedy ascent always reaches the largest cell in the grid

options.text: 0,0 only and then "steps 0 last 1", because the first cell has no larger neighbour to move to.
options.misconception: believes the walk ends at the first cell it visits without checking its neighbours

questions.explanation: The rule is that each step takes the larger of the two rising neighbours, and at 1,1 the cell below holds 8 against 7 on the right, so the walk goes down rather than right, which is why the sequence is 0,0 then 0,1, 1,1, 2,1, 2,2 and it halts there with 4 steps and a last value of 9. Expecting the climb to reach the 10 at 3,3 is tempting because a maximum looks reachable, but the walk is greedy rather than exhaustive: it commits to the larger neighbour each time and can stop while a larger cell sits behind a smaller one, which is a different question from asking for the largest cell overall.
questions.hint: At each cell, compare the two candidates before deciding to move.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Best on the path is not best in the grid
questions.learningObjective: compare the maximum reached by a greedy walk with the maximum of the whole grid

options.text: "6 100": the walk stopped at 6, because the 100 hides behind a neighbour of 1.
"100 100": a walk that always climbs to the larger neighbour must reach the largest cell.
options.misconception: believes stepping to the larger neighbour always reaches the grid maximum

options.text: "6 6": the whole-grid scan reuses the walk's stopping value as its own maximum.
options.misconception: believes the whole-grid scan is limited to the cells the walk visited

options.text: "100 6": the scan finds the 100 first in row-major order and the walk never improves on it.
options.misconception: believes the two printed values follow the order the maxima were found in

questions.explanation: The rule is that a walk which only steps to a larger neighbour can be trapped by a low cell in front of a high one, and here the walk reaches 6 at 1,1, where the cell below holds 1 and the cell right holds 3, so it stops even though 100 sits at 2,0, giving "6 100". Expecting the climb to find the tallest peak is tempting because the walk is a search for a maximum, but greedy ascent only promises a local result, and a maximum over a whole grid needs the full scan, which is the very loop sitting right beside the walk in this program.
questions.hint: Look at the two neighbours of the cell where the walk gave up.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A comparison that lets a tie move the walk
questions.learningObjective: predict how replacing > with >= changes a walk's route

options.text: 0,0 then 0,1, 0,2, 1,2 and "steps 3": an equal neighbour counts as rising, so the walk steps onto the tied 5.
0,0 then 0,1 and "steps 1": >= still refuses to move, because a tie is not a rise in value.
options.misconception: believes >= behaves like > when the two values are equal

options.text: 0,0 then 0,1, 0,2, 1,2, 2,2 and "steps 4": the walk also crosses the final column of the grid.
options.misconception: believes changing the comparison lets the walk leave the last row

options.text: It throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the second step, because a tie fails the bounds test.
options.misconception: believes comparing with >= makes the column bound test fail on a tie

questions.explanation: The rule is that >= treats an equal value as satisfying the test, so from 0,1 the tied 5 to the right now counts as a rise, the walk steps onto 0,2, and from there the 9 below is larger still, giving the route 0,0, 0,1, 0,2, 1,2 in 3 steps where the strict version stopped after one. Reading >= as harmless is tempting because the two operators look like a stylistic choice, but a walk defined as strictly rising uses that strictness to decide where it ends, and loosening it lets the walk wander across plateaus it was meant to refuse.
questions.hint: Compare the value at the cell to the right with the value under the walk.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: The bounds test before stepping down
questions.learningObjective: supply the row bound that makes a downward step legal on the last row

options.text: r + 1 < g.length  the test asks whether the row below exists before that row is read.
r + 1 <= g.length  the test includes the row just past the last index in the grid.
options.misconception: believes a row bound of length itself still names a real row

options.text: r < g.length  the test asks about the current row rather than the row underneath it.
options.misconception: believes the bound for row r + 1 is the bound that belongs to row r

options.text: c + 1 < g.length  the test asks whether the column below is present in the grid.
options.misconception: believes the row-below test should be written with the column bound

questions.explanation: The rule is that a row index is legal when it is smaller than the row count, so the row that is about to be read is r + 1 and its test is r + 1 < g.length, which is false here and leaves nr at 1 for the printed 1,0 best 5. Using <= is tempting because it looks like the familiar off-by-one guard, but a bound equal to the length names the row just past the end, so the guard lets the read through and the program dies with Index 2 out of bounds for length 2, and testing r instead of r + 1 fails in the same way one step too early.
questions.hint: The read uses r + 1, so the guard has to be about r + 1.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Turning a flat index into a cell
questions.learningObjective: map a row-major index onto a row and a column by division and remainder

options.text: p / cols  integer division by the width counts whole rows, and the remainder is the column.
p % cols  the remainder gives the row, and the quotient gives the column beside it.
options.misconception: believes the roles of quotient and remainder are swapped

options.text: cols / p  dividing the width by the index gives the row that the index belongs to.
options.misconception: believes dividing the width by the index locates the row

options.text: p - cols  subtracting one row's width from the index gives the row of the cell.
options.misconception: believes the row is the index minus a single row width

questions.explanation: The rule is that a row-major index is the row times the width plus the column, so integer division by the width recovers the row and the remainder recovers the column, which is why 5 divided by 3 gives row 1 and 5 mod 3 gives column 2, the cell holding 6. Subtracting the width is tempting because one subtraction looks like one row down, but it only works for the second row and drifts for every later one, and dividing the width by the index makes no sense at all once the index reaches the width, where it truncates to zero.
questions.hint: An index counts whole rows first, then columns within the row.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Cells visited by a greedy ascent
questions.learningObjective: count the cells a strictly rising walk stands on in a larger grid
questions.stem:
A walk starts at the top-left of the grid below, steps to a neighbour only when that neighbour is strictly larger, and stops when neither the cell to the right nor the cell below qualifies:
int[][] g = {
    {1, 5, 4, 5, 8},
    {2, 7, 9, 11, 8},
    {6, 6, 3, 13, 10},
    {3, 12, 12, 15, 14},
    {2, 9, 9, 17, 20}};
How many cells does the walk stand on, counting the starting cell? Respond with the integer only.
questions.explanation: Each step must go to a strictly larger cell, so the walk climbs 1 to 5 to 7 to 9 to 11 to 13 to 15 to 17 to 20 and only then finds that neither neighbour is larger, which is 9 cells. Reading the values in order and counting every rise is tempting because the grid is written in rows and the rising values do appear in a scattered order, but the walk moves one cell at a time in a single row or column, and a value such as the 12 in the fourth row is never reached because the 13 above-left of it was chosen instead.
questions.hint: Track the cell you are on; each move goes right or down, never back.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Best value along a listed path
questions.learningObjective: take the maximum of the grid cells named by a row-major path
questions.explanation: The rule is that a path only contributes the cells it actually names, and this path visits 4, 6, 9, 4, 3, and 8, so the largest of those is 9 and the 9 sitting at 0,1 is not on the path at all. Taking the last index to be the peak is tempting because a path is usually walked from start to end, but the order of the indexes carries no promise about the values, and the running best only ever grows, which is why 9 stays even after the walk visits the smaller 4, 3, and 8 at the end.
questions.hint: Convert each index with division by the width, then keep the largest value you meet.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Claims about a greedy ascent
questions.learningObjective: judge which statements hold for a walk that only steps to a larger cell
questions.stem: A study group debates four claims about a walk that starts at the top-left cell and only ever steps to a strictly larger neighbour, right or down. Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The walk can stop while a larger cell still sits somewhere else in the grid.
The value under the walk never decreases, since a step is only taken to a larger cell.
The last cell the walk reaches always holds the largest value in the whole grid.
options.misconception: believes a greedy ascent is guaranteed to reach the grid maximum

options.text: When two neighbours tie, the walk steps to whichever neighbour was tested first.
options.misconception: believes a tie sends the walk to the first neighbour tested

options.text: The walk visits every cell whose value exceeds the cell before it in reading order.
options.misconception: believes the ascent follows rising values in row-major order

questions.explanation: The rule is that a step happens only when a neighbour is strictly larger, so the values along the walk strictly increase, which proves the walk can end on a value that is not the grid's best, and also means the values never decrease. Reading the walk as a search is tempting because it does climb, but a tie gives no step at all under a strict test, so the walk halts rather than choosing a neighbour, and it never jumps ahead to a cell further along in reading order, so it misses rising values such as the 9 at 2,2 of the grid above.
questions.hint: Each move is justified by one comparison against the cell you are standing on.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A tie ends a strict ascent
questions.learningObjective: derive that the last cell of a strictly rising walk holds the path's maximum
questions.stem: A walk steps to a neighbour only when that neighbour holds a strictly larger value, and the cell to the right of the walk currently holds 5, exactly what the walk is standing on, while the cell below holds 2. Which statement about this walk is correct?

options.text: The walk stops there, and the largest value it has seen is the 5 it is standing on, since a tie is no rise.
The walk steps onto the equal neighbour, so the largest value it has seen becomes that tied 5.
options.misconception: believes a neighbour of equal value counts as a rise

options.text: The walk steps onto the equal neighbour and keeps going, so it visits both of the tied 5s.
options.misconception: believes the walk continues past a tie by looking further ahead

options.text: The walk ignores the equal neighbour but scans the rest of its row for something larger.
options.misconception: believes the walk scans a whole row rather than taking one step

questions.explanation: The rule is that every step strictly increases the value, so the sequence of values along the walk rises all the way to the cell where it stops, which makes that final cell the maximum of the path; with a neighbour of 5 beside a current 5 the strict test is false, so no step is taken and the walk ends on 5. Stepping onto the tie is tempting because 5 is not smaller, but strictly larger is the whole condition, and a walk that allowed equal steps could wander over a plateau forever without ever gaining height, which is why the test is written with > rather than >=.
questions.hint: Every accepted step raises the current value, so the last one is the highest.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A path walk that skips its first cell
questions.learningObjective: find the maximum reported by a path walk that never visits the starting cell

options.text: It prints 4, because the loop starts at index 1 and never looks at path[0], which held the 9.
It prints 9, because the MIN_VALUE seed is replaced by the first cell the loop reaches.
options.misconception: believes the MIN_VALUE seed is overwritten by the starting cell

options.text: It throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because path[0] is never validated before the loop.
options.misconception: believes skipping the first cell makes the path read leave the grid

options.text: It prints 0, because a running maximum reports zero when no cell exceeds the seed.
options.misconception: believes a MIN_VALUE seed is reported as zero when nothing beats it

questions.explanation: The rule is that a maximum over a path has to consider every cell on it, and this loop begins at i = 1, so the starting cell is never read and the largest value it does see is 4, even though the path begins on 9. Trusting the seed is tempting because Integer.MIN_VALUE is the safest possible starting value, but the seed only guarantees a correct answer if the first cell is actually compared against it, and starting the loop at 1 means the 9 is not in the comparison set at all rather than being lost to a bad initial value.
questions.hint: Count how many of the path's cells the loop body ever reads.
